newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU panel calls for social spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: German CDU panel calls for social spending cuts.

text.p: An economic committee of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Wednesday urged the government to cut spending further on unemployment, pensions and bureaucrats.

Such cuts are needed as Germany continues toward its goal of slimming the state's share of the economy to 46 percent by the year 2000, the panel's chairman, Dieter Murmann, told reporters. The state share has climbed steadily since German unification in 1990, and is now just over 50 percent.

Apart from the need to trim the budget deficit to qualify for European monetary union, Germany has been trying to cut taxes and spending in parallel to reduce the role of the state in the economy and give greater freedom to the private sector.
But at a time of high unemployment, resistance to the spending cuts is strong, as shown by demonstrations this week by police and other public-sector workers in Bonn.
Murmann said Germany will need to cut 125 billion marks ($72.8 billion) in total spending by the year 2000 to achieve this goal.

Shortfalls in tax revenues make the task harder, Murmann said, but he endorsed the government's proposed tax reform, which aims at net tax cuts of up to 30 billion marks, and said he opposed tax increases.
The panel's recommendations, which could influence future budgets, include limiting unemployment benefits to 12 months, and a cap on additional spending for job-creation schemes.
Unemployed people who take part in retraining programmes should receive half the cost of such courses in the form of loans that must be repaid.

The German public sector, which now employs over six million workers, should shed 600,000 jobs in the next three years, which will be possible mainly through attrition, said panel member Ruediger von Voss.
Bureaucrats' pensions should also be reduced by six percentage points, in stages, from the current level of 75 percent of final salary.
Pension reform should be accelerated to start in 1998, with the planned reduction in pensions to 64 percent of salary achieved by 2010.
Further spending cuts could be achieved in health insurance and long-term care insurance, the panel said.
-- Terence Gallagher, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($ = 1.716 German Marks)
